Milestones that
Shaped Our Legacy
2019-Present
Global horizons and new ventures
While expanding across sectors such as Government, Telecom, and Retail, Posidex set its sights on the global stage in 2023. Our commitment to innovation led us to the NAM and MENA markets, establishing offices in Canada and Dubai. With each new step, we continue to transform how businesses worldwide understand and engage with their customers.
2014-2018
Innovation at scale
Our innovative spirit led to the launch of breakthrough products like Posilytics for data analytics and the Watchlist Screening Application. We also ventured into new technological frontiers, embracing Big Data, Machine Learning, and Cloud solutions, paving the way for the future of contextual customer insights.
2012-2013
Expanding impact
With a growing reputation, we saw a surge in clientele from India's largest NBFCs, insurance and private sector banks. This period of growth marked the beginning of our deep partnerships and expanding footprint across major sectors.
2008-2011
Recognition and reach
Our relentless pursuit of innovation brought us accolades, including winning the RFP for India’s largest data mining exercise for the Central Government, the Prime Minister’s Award for our ITDMS solution, and the ITsAP Award for Research and Innovation. These honors solidified our position as pioneers in customer data management solutions.
2006-2007
Opening new frontiers
Our journey gained momentum with the sale of our first license to a leading private-sector bank. Our entry into the NBFC and insurance sectors broadened our horizons and demonstrated the adaptability of our solutions across various industries.
2003-2005
The genesis
Posidex was born out of a vision to simplify the chaos of customer data. In our early days, we undertook India’s largest deduplication exercise, proving our expertise in data management. This milestone laid the foundation for our flagship product, which entered beta testing and set the stage for a data revolution.

Customer Data Platform vs Master Data Management
Table Of Contents
MDM vs CDP: Major differences and benefits
Customer Data Platforms and Master Data Management (cdp and mdm) are two different concepts with similar names. Both customer data platforms and master data management (cdp and mdm) are in the business of collecting, storing, analysing and exposing the data to the business users who can use it to make better business decisions. With a rising number of businesses looking to implement a Customer Data Platform, it is important to understand the difference (mdm vs cdp) between the two. This blog will look at what they are and what makes them different.
The major challenge faced by Enterprises in a data-rich environment is managing and getting reliable customer data that drives accurate business decisions. A common enterprise mdm solutions platform is very important to help in organising and managing customer data that flows in from multi-channels at boundless speed and unlimited variety. Enterprise Customer Data Platforms and Enterprise Mdm solutions are two such platforms on which enterprises can rely on for storing, transforming, and unifying customer data to make computations easier and processes more agile.
MDM vs CDP
Customer Master data management
(MDM) is a process designed to manage and transform organisation-wide data. On the other hand, Customer Data Platform (CDP) is a product that specifically improves customization of customer data. Customer Data Platforms and Master Data Management (CDP and MDM) both work together to deliver solutions such as single view of the customer, screening of customer data etc.
What is an MDM solution VS CDP Solution?
MDM solutions enable technology to work in alignment with business to ensure uniformity, accuracy, stewardship, semantic consistency, and accountability in all the shared enterprise master data assets. Thus, it includes the processes, approaches, and technologies that are used to manage important shared data within an organisation. CDP solutions can be built exclusively for manipulating and managing customer data. These solutions are packaged software built for different business use cases, such as marketing, analytics, customer service and delight, etc. Since CDP is a prebuilt and pre-configured system, it does not require high level technical skills for business users to use data, reducing time, cost and expertise resources in enterprises.
Main aim of MDM Vs CDP
The main aim of MDM is to deliver a ‘master record’ that is accurate, reliable, and consistent across all pooled business data, thus, allowing different departments within the enterprise to work with appropriate data that meets their individual requirements from among the volumes of shared data.
The main aim of the CDP is to deliver a coherent, trustworthy, and persistent ‘Golden Record’ from different data sources to empower the marketing and operations teams to work with business data without the need of IT team or engineers.
Accessibility of MDM Vs CDP
There is only one true Master Data for an Enterprise that is stored in MDM. The repository can be tricky to manage by other departments and therefore, must be managed by
enterprise MDM solutions
engineers only.
Inversely, data stored in the CDP can be used by other systems for analysis and to manage customer interactions.
Data view of MDM Vs CDP
MDM is a heterogeneous pooled data from different touchpoints such as department, channel, or aspect of an organisation to be represented in one place and create a ‘single source of truth.’ Though it may represent the address of details of the company data pipeline, it might not necessarily give a complete view of each customer.
CDP on the other hand can give a comprehensive view of each customer creating a ‘single customer view’ of the customer linking the relationships and information from multiple systems.
Applications in MDM Vs CDP
MDM facilitates collection, storing and sharing of enterprise data. It may not be ideal for other transformations as the main purpose of MDM is to provide a single source of truth for the data.
CDP deals with customer data, and allows collecting, cleansing, de-duplicating, storing, matching, and screening of data according to business needs.
Benefits of MDM Vs CDP
MDM
‍
1. Global: One true global, centralised data for consistency in applications.
2. MDM is an agile platform that can be easily expandable to new channels to get high-quality information from a variety of sources.
3. MDM enables delivery of a trusted version of data that supports business initiatives.
4. MDM data is agnostic to specific business application landscape and is applicable to any adopted implementations by the end-user organisations.
5. A golden record system may support any solution that can be customised across industries to address specific challenges.
‍
CDP
1. CDP can handle all kinds of data that can be transformed into various formats.
2. CDP gives real-time accessibility to customer data that can be easily and quickly accessed with powerful ML and AI driven technologies for immediate powerful implementations.
3. CDP is cross-functional and flexible to access data and tools across departments within an organisation.
4. CDP enables comprehensive customer view, relationship connects, and seamless integrations of data.
5. CDP’s single view of customer data combined with technology can also be highly scalable to handle billions of consumer records per day.

Cross-system data management can be challenging, but deduplication can help. In this Blog, we’ll explore what deduplication is, how it works, how to select the best data deduplication software, and some options to choose from. We live in a data-driven world where organizations are generating and storing more data than ever before. As a result, managing and storing this massive amount of data has become a significant challenge for many organisations. One of the challenges that organisations face is data duplication, which can result in wasted storage space and increased storage costs.  To address this challenge, many organisations are turning to data deduplication software solutions. In this blog post, we will explore what data deduplication is and how data deduplication software can benefit organisations. We will also discuss how Data deduplication works, methods and learn about secure data deduplication services.
What is Data Deduplication?
Data deduplication is a process that identifies and eliminates duplicate data within a system or network. It is a technique that helps to reduce storage requirements and backup times by identifying and removing redundant data. Duplicate data can be caused by various reasons, including multiple versions of files or backups, data migrations, or data replication. Data deduplication software solutions are designed to identify these duplicates and remove them while maintaining data integrity. When looking for data deduplication solutions, it’s important to compare data deduplication vendors to find the best fit for your needs.
How does Data Deduplication work?
Data deduplication is a technique that involves identifying and removing duplicate data from a storage system. This process can help reduce storage costs and improve system performance.
The process of data deduplication works by first identifying duplicate data within a storage system. This can be achieved through a variety of techniques, such as comparing data blocks or using hashing algorithms.
Once the duplicate data has been identified, it is either removed or replaced with a reference to the original data. This means that only one copy of the data is stored, rather than multiple copies of the same data.
By choosing reliable data deduplication vendors, you can streamline your data storage and management processes.
Why is Data Deduplication Important?​
Data deduplication is important for several reasons.
Firstly,
it helps to reduce storage requirements and backup times, which can lead to significant cost savings for organizations.
Secondly
it helps to improve data protection by reducing the amount of data that needs to be backed up or replicated.
Thirdly
, it can improve the overall performance of systems and networks by reducing the amount of data that needs to be processed.
Data Deduplication Methods
There are several methods of data deduplication that can be employed depending on the needs of the organisation.
File-Level Deduplication
This method identifies duplicate files and replaces them with a pointer to the original file. This approach is useful for situations where multiple users have identical copies of the same file.
Block-Level Deduplication
This method breaks data into small chunks or blocks, and each block is compared to a repository of blocks to see if it already exists. If it does, a pointer to the existing block is created, otherwise, the new block is stored. This approach is useful when a single file contains many similar blocks of data.
Source-Based Deduplication
This method is used to eliminate duplicate data at the source, typically a remote office or branch location, before it is sent to the central data centre. This approach is useful when bandwidth is limited and network traffic needs to be minimized.
Inline and Post-Process Deduplication
Inline deduplication identifies and eliminates duplicate data as it is being written to disk, while post-process deduplication identifies and eliminates duplicate data after it has been written to disk. Inline deduplication is typically faster, but post-process deduplication can be more efficient.
Global Deduplication
This method compares data across multiple devices, locations, or even organisations, to identify and eliminate duplicate data. This approach is useful when data is replicated across multiple locations or devices. Each of these data deduplication methods has its own advantages and disadvantages, and the most appropriate method will depend on the specific needs and goals of the organisation.
Dedupe in Banking
Dedupe, short for data deduplication, is a crucial process in the banking industry that helps identify and eliminate duplicate customer records. This is important because duplicate records can lead to inconsistencies in customer data, making it difficult for banks to provide accurate and timely services. By implementing dedupe in banking, financial institutions can improve their customer data management processes, reduce errors, and increase operational efficiency. This not only helps improve customer satisfaction but also reduces the risk of fraud and compliance issues. Overall, dedupe in banking is an essential tool for banks looking to streamline their data management processes and provide high-quality services to their customers.
Customer Data Deduplication Softwares
Customer data deduplication software helps organisations to remove duplicate data from their customer databases.
These software solutions use sophisticated algorithms and matching techniques to identify duplicate records, taking into account variations in data such as misspellings, abbreviations, and different formats. Once duplicates are identified, the software allows users to merge or delete them as needed.
There are many different customer data deduplication software solutions available on the market, each with its own unique features and capabilities. Organizations should evaluate their needs and choose a solution that best fits their specific requirements, taking into account factors such as data volume, complexity, and integration with existing systems.

Understanding the Differences Between Data Mesh vs Data Fabric
Table Of Contents
In the realm of data management and architecture, two prominent approaches have emerged:
Data Mesh vs Data Fabric
While both aim to address the challenges of managing and leveraging data in complex environments, they employ distinct principles and methodologies. In this blog post, we will delve into the nuances of Data fabric vs Data Mesh architectures, highlighting the difference between data fabric data mesh.
Data Mesh vs Data Fabric
Data Fabric and Data Mesh are two contrasting architectural paradigms that offer different perspectives on organizing and utilizing data within an organization. Let’s explore the fundamental difference between Data Fabric Data Mesh.
Data Mesh
Empowering Decentralized Data Ownership
Data Mesh emphasizes the distribution of data ownership and management across
cross-functional teams
or domains. This decentralized approach promotes autonomy and agility by empowering individual teams to take ownership of their data domains. Rather than relying on a centralized data governance model, Data Mesh encourages teams to build their own data products and define their
data pipelines
within their domains.
Data Fabric
Unifying Data Infrastructure
In contrast, Data Fabric is a centralized architecture that seeks to create a unified and
integrated data infrastructure
. It provides a holistic view of data assets and enables seamless data integration, access, and governance. Data Fabric aims to abstract the underlying complexities of data management, providing a unified layer that connects disparate data sources and applications. It offers a cohesive framework for data orchestration, governance, and access control. Data fabric relies on metadata to connect and link data assets and users.
Differences Between Data Fabric vs Data Mesh Architectures
When considering data architecture options, it’s important to evaluate the differences between data fabric vs data mesh architectures. When comparing Data Mesh and Data Fabric architectures, several key differentiators emerge. The choice between data fabric vs data mesh architectures depends on factors such as organizational structure, data complexity, and the need for scalability, as each approach offers unique advantages and trade-offs.
Data Ownership and Governance
Data Mesh promotes decentralized data ownership, enabling individual teams to govern their respective data domains independently. Each team takes responsibility for the data quality, availability, and access within their domain. In contrast, Data Fabric emphasizes centralized
data governance
, enforcing consistent standards and policies across the entire organization.
Data Integration and Connectivity Data
Fabric provides a centralized approach to data integration, facilitating seamless connectivity between various data sources, applications, and systems. It offers pre-built connectors and tools for data ingestion, transformation, and integration. Data Mesh, on the other hand, focuses on data productization and encourages teams to build their own data pipelines and integrations within their domains. This allows for more flexibility and agility but requires individual teams to handle their integration challenges.
Scalability and Agility
Data Mesh architecture inherently enables scalability and agility as individual teams can independently scale and evolve their data products. They can adapt their data pipelines, schemas, and processing logic according to their specific needs, allowing for faster iteration and innovation. In contrast, Data Fabric provides a unified platform that offers scalability and agility at an enterprise level, catering to the organization as a whole. It ensures consistent scalability and standardized processes across different data domains.
Vendor Landscape
Both Data Mesh and Data Fabric have gained attention in the industry, resulting in the emergence of vendors offering specialized solutions for each architecture. Organizations considering these approaches can explore various data mesh vendors and data fabric vendors to find suitable tools and technologies that align with their architectural requirements. It is important to evaluate the data mesh vendors expertise, support, and integration capabilities while choosing between the many data mesh vendors.
Summary
Data fabric vs data mesh architectures presents contrasting approaches to data management, with data fabric emphasizing centralized governance and standardization, while data mesh promotes decentralized ownership and autonomy.
Choosing the right data architecture is crucial for organizations seeking to unlock the full potential of their data assets. While Data Fabric and Data Mesh share a common goal of effective data management, they differ significantly in their principles, governance models, and integration approaches. Understanding the difference between Data Fabric and Data Mesh will help organizations make informed decisions and adopt the most suitable architecture for their specific needs and objectives.

Decentralized Data Management: Data Democratization, Data Fabric, and Data Mesh
Decentralized data management refers to a system where data is managed on a domain basis, with individual departments or teams taking more responsibility instead of a centralized body.
This approach is supported by three key terms:
data democratization, data fabric, and data mesh.
Data democratization
is a philosophy where everyone in the organization is held responsible for the production, use, and quality of data, rather than just a single role or department. The focus is on providing users with greater access to data, data literacy, and data culture.
Data fabric
is a data management solution that connects all data sources and management components through metadata, creating a frictionless web that provides access to enterprise data to all relevant stakeholders. Data fabric has the potential to develop a user-friendly and largely autonomous enterprise-wide data coverage interface when it is fully integrated.
Data mesh
is a decentralized architecture and governance concept that puts responsibility for data on the teams that produce and own the data. While still incorporating some centralized governance principles to prevent data from becoming siloed, data mesh empowers teams to be more autonomous in managing their data.
Decentralized approaches offer benefits such as:
More immediate decision-making2
More power to end-users
Creation of data products that require no preparation.
However, they also present challenges in data management a to achieve a decentralized data management landscape, organizations need tools that can
Collect metadata
Provide data access to everyone
Combine multiple tools into a single, user-friendly platform.

Data quality is an ever-evolving field, and organizations have adopted different approaches to tackle it. In the past, a rule-based approach was common, and later, AI and machine learning techniques were used to identify low-quality data.
However, new big data management trends are emerging, which take a holistic approach to data quality by employing various techniques to monitor data health. Data observability refers to one of the many master data management industry trends.
Data observability
is the ability of an organization to understand the state of its data based on the information collected by monitoring the system via automation with minimal manual intervention. With data observability, organizations can recognize:
Data quality issues
Anomalies Schema changes
Schema changes
More about their entire data systems
The benefits of data observability include the
Ability to monitor data systems with little to no domain knowledge
Proactively detect issues
Handle more complex data systems.
AI-driven data quality is also gaining traction. AI algorithms can automate the identification of data quality issues and provide recommendations for resolution. AI-driven data quality can help organizations identify patterns and make predictions that may not be apparent to humans. By automating data quality processes, organizations can detect issues faster and with more accuracy.
This is one of the new trends in data management in 2023.

Data Governance vs. Data Management
Table Of Contents
Making Sense of Two Essential Concepts
Data management vs Data Governance
In the world of data, two important concepts often arise – Data Governance and Data Management. While both data management and governance play a crucial role in ensuring the effectiveness and efficiency of data usage in organizations, they often cause confusion, as they are often used interchangeably.
The truth is, Data management and governance are two distinct concepts, with their own set of processes and objectives.
In this blog, we’ll dive into the differences between Data Governance and Data Management, and also learn about data quality and data governance, data governance and master data management and enterprise data governance management.
Whether you’re new to the data world or have years of experience, this guide will provide a clear understanding of these two important concepts and their impact on data management.
What is Data Governance?
Data Governance refers to the policies, procedures, and standards that define how data is created, used, and protected within an organisation. It provides a framework for ensuring the accuracy, consistency, and security of data, and it establishes who is responsible for making decisions about data management and use.
What is Data Management?
Data Management, on the other hand, encompasses the processes and tools used to collect, store, and maintain data. This includes data warehousing, database management, data integration, and data quality management. Data management is concerned with ensuring that the data is accurate, accessible, and secure, but it doesn’t address the broader governance issues of who has the authority to use or modify the data.
Data management vs Data Governance?
Let’s understand with the help of an example!
Now lets checkout data management vs data governance main differences in real time. Consider a large retail company that collects data on customer purchases, demographics, and product information.
Data Governance
in this situation would involve establishing policies and procedures for the creation, usage, and protection of customer data. This might include defining who is responsible for managing customer data, how customer data can be used, and how customer data will be protected. The company might also establish a data governance board to oversee decisions related to customer data and ensure that data policies are being followed.
Data Management
in this situation would involve the processes and tools used to collect, store, and maintain the customer data. This might include setting up a data warehouse to store customer data, implementing data quality management processes to ensure the accuracy of customer data, and implementing data security measures to protect sensitive information. The goal of data management in this situation is to ensure that the customer data is accessible, accurate, and secure.
Data Quality and Data Governance
Effective Master Data Management requires a solid Data Governance framework to ensure the accuracy, completeness, and consistency of master data across the organisation. By combining data governance and master data management, organisations can ensure that their master data is of high quality, properly managed, and consistently used across the organisation, leading to better decision making and improved operational efficiency.
Data Governance and Master Data Management
Effective Data Governance can play a critical role in ensuring data quality, by establishing a set of standards and processes for collecting and maintaining data. This includes implementing data quality management practices, such as data profiling, data cleaning, and data standardisation, to ensure the accuracy and consistency of data across an organisation. By combining data quality and data governance practices, organisations can be confident in the quality and security of their data assets and use this data to make informed business decisions.
Enterprise Data Governance Management
This enterprise data governance management framework typically involves the creation of a data governance board or committee, responsible for making decisions related to data usage and management. Together, Enterprise Data Governance and Data Management provide a comprehensive approach to managing an organisation’s data assets and ensuring that data is used effectively and efficiently to support business objectives.
Summary
While comparing data management vs data governance, both the data management and governance are critical for organisations, they serve different purposes and address different challenges. Effective data governance provides a clear framework for making decisions about data management, while robust data management processes ensure that data is accurate, secure, and accessible.

What is Customer Master Data Management?
Master Data Management Customer
or Customer master data management (CMDM) is the process of creating a centralized, single view of customer data. This data may come from multiple sources, both internal and external to the organization. CMDM ensures that this customer data is accurate, consistent, and up-to-date. It also provides a single source of truth for all customer data, which can be used by various departments within the organization.
The benefits of CMDM include improved customer service, better decision-making, and increased operational efficiency. When customer data is managed effectively, organizations can provide a better customer experience and improve their relationships with customers. Additionally, CMDM can help organizations to make better decisions by providing accurate and up-to-date data. Finally, CMDM can help to increase operational efficiency by reducing the need for manual data entry and improving data quality.

Customer data management solution helps
improve customer relationships

Customer data management platform
improves efficiency
within an organisation by reducing duplicates and errors in customer data, which can save time and resources.
Customer data management solution

regulations, such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the other Privacy Acts by providing a clear view of customer data and allowing for easy deletion or anonymization of data upon request.
Customer data management platform

of their customer base by providing insights into customer demographics, purchasing patterns, and preferences.

marketing automation and analytics platforms
.
Accuracy, Completeness and Consistency
Customer Master Data Management / master data management customer (CMDM) is a process that ensures the accuracy, completeness, and consistency of customer data across an organisation. It is crucial for businesses to have a clear understanding of their customer base in order to make informed decisions and provide a seamless customer experience. In this guide, we will cover the importance of CMDM, the steps involved in implementing a CMDM system, and best practices for maintaining and utilizing customer data.
The importance of a
customer data management platform
can be seen in the potential consequences of inaccurate or inconsistent customer data.
For example, if a business sends a marketing email to the wrong address, it not only wastes resources, but also risks damaging the customer relationship. Additionally, duplicate customer records can lead to confusion and inefficiencies in customer service and sales. A
CMDM system
helps to avoid these issues by providing a single, accurate source of customer information.
Implementing a CMDM system involves several steps:k
Step 1:
Collection
The first step is data collection, which involves gathering customer information from various sources within the organisation, such as sales and customer service departments.
‍
Step 2: Consolidation
The data is cleaned and consolidated to ensure accuracy and completeness. This includes removing duplicates, correcting errors, and standardising formatting. Once the data is cleaned and consolidated, it is then integrated into a central repository, such as a CRM or ERP system. This allows for easy access and updates to customer information by all relevant departments.
‍
Step 3: ERP
The final step in implementing a CMDM system is to establish procedures for data maintenance and usage. This includes regular data updates, monitoring for errors and inconsistencies, and training employees on how to use the system.
Monitoring Errors and Inconsistencies
In addition to implementing a CMDM system, there are several best practices for maintaining and utilizing customer data. One important practice is to keep customer data up to date. This includes regularly collecting new information and updating existing information as necessary. It is also important to monitor the data for errors and inconsistencies, and to have a process in place for addressing them.
Another best practice is to ensure that customer data is being used effectively. This includes training employees on how to access and use the data, and ensuring that the data is being used to inform business decisions. Additionally, it is important to consider the various ways in which customer data can be used, such as in marketing and customer service.
Encryption and Access
Finally, it is essential to protect customer data from unauthorised access or breaches. This includes implementing security measures such as encryption and regularly reviewing access permissions.
Customer MDM in the Cloud

This allows organizations to create, maintain and access a centralized, accurate, and consistent view of customer data in a cloud-based environment.

Increased Data Integrity

India’s DPDP Act Is In Place: Is Your Organization Ready?
Table Of Contents
Data is both the fuel and the foundation of business growth.
But with growing volumes of sensitive customer information and the introduction of the
Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP)
Act, 2023, data protection has become a boardroom priority.
As its implementation nears, enterprises must ask themselves a critical question:Is your organization ready to comply (and compete) in this new data protection era?
‍
Understanding the DPDP Act: What It Means for Businesses
The Act applies to any organization that collects or processes the digital personal data of Indian citizens, whether in India or abroad.
It
defines personal data
as any information that can identify an individual, including names, financial details, identification numbers, biometric data or health details.
Modeled after global privacy frameworks such as the GDPR and CCPA, the DPDP Act places the individual (known as the Data Principal), not the organization, at the center of the data ecosystem.
At its core, the law emphasizes consent, purpose limitation, and accountability. Organizations must:
Collect only the data necessary for a specific purpose,
Use it transparently,
And store it securely.
Any data breach or unauthorized exposure can trigger severe penalties, up to ₹250 crore ( ~ USD 28M) per occurrence, along with reputational damage and loss of customer trust.
‍
THE ACT MANDATES KEY COMPLIANCE REQUIREMENTS
1. Breach notification
Mandatory reporting of data breaches to the Data Protection Board and affected individuals.
2. Data minimization
Organizations must only retain data for as long as necessary for the intended purpose.
3. Consent-based data processing
Explicit, informed consent must be obtained before collecting or sharing personal data.
‍
For a business, these requirements call for more than just policy updates.
They demand a new architecture for data security and protection.
Because the act asks for implementation of security measures like encryption, obfuscation, masking or the use of virtual tokens.
Companies also need to maintain access controls and access logs. They would also need to review and monitor the access logs regularly to detect any unauthorised activity
‍
The Compliance Challenge: Where Organizations Struggle
While most enterprises have basic data protection measures in place, these traditional methods are often not enough to meet the evolving compliance and operational needs under DPDP.
Fragmented data landscape:
Sprawling PII across legacy, cloud, and AI systems. It increases the surface area for breaches and unauthorized access. Given that
India has become the 2nd most targeted nation
for cyber-attacks globally, data minimization is necessary.
The encryption paradox
: Another challenge lies in the paradox of modern data usage. Organizations must analyse and process vast amounts of sensitive data for real-time decisions and to deliver personalization. But to process the data, they need to decrypt it, which compromises DPDPA compliance.
This is where many legacy systems fall short.
What’s needed is a privacy-by-design approach.
One that integrates protection into every stage of the data lifecycle.
‍
What is a data vault?
A data privacy vault acts as a secure repository for sensitive data that keeps it safe from unauthorized access and eases compliance with data regulations without sacrificing data utility
‍
The Bottom Line
Compliance with laws like DPDPA is often seen as a cost.
But with a data vault it can become a catalyst for trust and business growth.
Customers are increasingly choosing brands that protect their data and respect their privacy. With a data vault, businesses can do both. Turning compliance into a competitive edge.
‍

Keeping Pace with Continuous Changes in the Regulatory Space
Table Of Contents
As technology evolves, fraudsters adapt to it, making it imperative for the banking, financial services, and insurance (BFSI) sector to
continuously
improve their defence mechanisms. With regulators intensifying their norms, be it anti-money laundering (AML) or counter-terrorist financing (CTF), businesses also need
solid
know-your-customer (KYC) and customer due diligence (CDD) processes.
Over and above it, they need compliance to be double-edged: real-time vigilance and periodic checks.
‍
THE DUAL FACETS OF COMPLIANCE
The primary objective of KYC and the more holistic CDD is to prevent banks, fintechs, and FIs from being exploited for financial fraud, money laundering schemes, or any other illegal activities. This means not only vetting and screening new customers as they are onboarded but also monitoring existing customers on an ongoing basis for any suspicious activities.
‍
WHAT MOST BFSI PLAYERS FOCUS ON
Most businesses earmark their attention on identity verification during customer onboarding because laws demand it.
In the USA, financial institutions must comply with the
USA Patriot Act's
CIP, the Bank Secrecy Act’s KYC, and AML requirements, including OFAC screening and identity verification. In Canada, institutions must follow
PCMLTFA
regulations, involving customer and beneficial owner verification, KYC, and reporting to
FINTRAC
. Both countries emphasise documentation, ongoing monitoring, and enhanced due diligence for PEPs and
HIO
s.
In India, besides the
Master Directions on KYC by Reserve Bank of India
, BFSIs must follow the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA).
In MENA, compliance is shaped by directives from the UAE Central Bank (CBUAE) AML/CFT guidelines, Saudi Arabia’s SAMA regulations, and FATF-aligned supervisory frameworks across GCC states. Institutions must implement robust KYC/CDD, and screening against local and international sanction lists while ensuring adherence to UAE PDPL and Saudi NCA requirements.
In Southeast Asia, MAS Notices (Singapore), BNM’s AMLA framework (Malaysia), and OJK/PPATK requirements (Indonesia) must be followed for AML/CFT along with real-time KYC, ongoing CDD, and suspicious transaction reporting.
Using advanced
technologies like real-time entity search and match,
they instantly search and verify customer documents. It streamlines the KYC process and safeguards against potential threats at the speed businesses require today
‍
Compliance Blind Spots Are Expensive
But this focus often narrows to only one side of the compliance road. It’s equivalent to putting guardrails on just one side of the road, leaving the other wide open to threats.
True compliance demands full-lane protection: Forward Scan (real-time screening at onboarding), Reverse Scan (screening your entire existing customer base against new entries in watchlists), and Rescan (continuous, automated monitoring as watchlists evolve).
And you need to run these checks across your entire dataset in a cost-effective way, ensuring nothing slips through the cracks.
‍
WHAT THEY OVERLOOK
If real-time checks during onboarding constitute one facet of compliance, recurring screening cadences constitute the other. Periodically screening and monitoring existing customers adds another layer of vigilance, ensuring sustained integrity and continuous adherence to evolving regulations.
‍
ReKYC is crucial as businesses and customers evolve over time.
You may expand to a new area with new laws becoming applicable, or the very nature of your customer may change due to employment or relocations.
They may also become a politically exposed person (PEP) or be associated with them, requiring sanction screening and enhanced due diligence (EDD), especially considering the current evolving political environment across the world.
So, your compliance regime needs to be up-to-date and continuous.
‍
A SHORT CASE IN POINT
Consider Bank A, which decided to put compliance on the back burner and release new products and services quickly. It allowed them to keep costs low and expand into new customer segments. A year down the line, regulatory bodies slapped them with a fine.
Another year later, regulators clamped down on part of the services because the bank failed to check that multiple customers used the same identity card.
The consequence? Compliance costs and effort went through the roof, customers left, stock deteriorated, and the bank’s reputation was forever marred.
‍
If the bank had invested in a simple batch-mode
Customer Linking and Identification Process tool
right at the start, they could have conducted daily periodic checks in bulk. It would identify duplicate records and report any occurring changes, fortifying their compliance –
continuously
.
‍
All of this needs to happen keeping Customer Experience in mind
In addition to being two-pronged, compliance processes must cover the 2 ends of the scale: insufficient checks and customer experience (CX).
‍
In this digital world, where services are graded in the court of public opinion, customer experience is the next competitive battlefield. Neglecting increasingly stringent compliance norms is not an option. Neither is poor customer experience.
‍
Poorly designed processes lead to poor CX.
A lengthy and confusing identity verification process in fintech can push customers to abandon. At a big bank, the same queries for information to meet complex KYC requirements from different departments can cause customer frustration.
‍
Quick, non-intrusive, & thorough CDD
While traditional AML checks and KYC processes form the foundation of customer due diligence, they are no longer sufficient in isolation. To truly safeguard your business, BFSIs need to adopt a multi-layered approach that goes beyond vanilla compliance measures.
A comprehensive CDD strategy should include rigorous, multiple layers of scrutiny, ensuring that every aspect of a customer's profile is thoroughly vetted.
Multi-Database Checks
: screening customers against a wide array of global watchlists, government sanction lists, financial litigation records, and internal blacklists.
Ultimate Beneficiary Ownership (UBO) Checks
: While AML is a cornerstone of CDD, it alone is not sufficient to capture the full spectrum of risks. During the opening of corporate bank accounts, it is crucial to identify the ultimate beneficiaries to uncover hidden interests and ensure transparency in financial transactions.
Real-Time Transaction Monitoring
: Through N-tier, graph-based analyses that map the sphere of influence are essential to detect and respond to suspicious activities promptly.

Master Data Management (MDM) is the process of managing and consolidating data from multiple sources into a single, accurate, and up-to-date view of an organization’s critical data. Learn the basics of master data management solutions and how it can help organizations improve data quality and make better decisions. We’ll also provide an overview of MDM tools and how they can be used to support MDM initiatives.
What is MDM Master Data Management?
Master Data Management (MDM) is the process of managing your customer data from its source to ensure that it’s up to date and that you have a single consistent version of customer records.
Why is Master Data Management important?
Data is the foundation for making any business decisions and it’s important to manage it well to ensure that the data is relevant, reliable, and insightful for the business.
How MDM helps your business?
Master data management (MDM) is specifically designed to connect with your customer and understand the customer better to develop your business products and innovations. Creating an MDM single source of truth within an organization can help in better customer experience, compliance, reporting, and many other critical business operations.
Which MDM solution is the best for you?
While Master Data Management (MDM) is one of the most important data management strategies, selecting the right product for your business needs is a very necessary step. There are numerous MDM products with a unique set of features and the product that works best for you will depend on several factors including the business, purpose, and goals.

What Is Master Data Governance And Why Do You Need It?
Table Of Contents
MDG Master Data Governance is a comprehensive framework and model that helps organizations establish control over their critical master data assets.
In today’s data-driven business landscape, the effective management of master data has become crucial for organizations to drive operational efficiency, improve decision-making, and ensure data integrity. This blog explores the concept of MDG master data governance, master data governance framework, master data governance model, its benefits, capabilities, and best practices, highlighting why it is essential for modern businesses.
What is Master Data Governance?
MDG Master Data Governance refers to the
Processes
Policies
Technologies
implemented to ensure
Accuracy
Consistency
Reliability
of an organization’s master data.
Master data represents core business entities such as
customers, products, suppliers, and employees
which are shared across multiple systems and business units. Master data governance model aims to establish a centralized governance framework to manage this critical data consistently throughout its lifecycle.
(MDM vs. MDG )Master Data Management vs Master Data Governance
While Master Data Management (MDM) focuses on creating a single, trusted view of master data across the enterprise, MDG goes a step further by providing the governance framework and processes to maintain the quality and integrity of that data. MDM handles data integration, harmonization, and data quality, while MDG ensures ongoing governance, data stewardship, and compliance. MDM data governance is the collective attribute that can be attributed to both.
Master Data Management
Focuses on the management and control of an organization’s master data.
Involves creating a centralized and consistent source of truth for master data.
Deals with data integration, data quality, data modeling, data storage, and data governance.Includes processes, policies, and technologies to ensure data consistency and accuracy.
Provides a framework for data sharing, collaboration, and decision-making across different departments or systems.
Enables data stewardship, data ownership, and data lifecycle management.
Master Data Governance
Focuses on the governance and control of an organization’s master data. Involves defining and enforcing policies, rules, and processes for managing master data. Deals with data ownership, data security, data privacy, and compliance with regulations. Includes establishing data governance roles, responsibilities, and workflows. Provides a framework for data quality management, data access controls, and data change management. Enables data accountability, data transparency, and data governance maturity.
It is important to note that master data governance is a subset of master data management. While master data management focuses on the overall management of master data, master data governance specifically addresses the governance aspects of managing master data
Benefits and Capabilities of Master Data Governance
Master data governance model offers several benefits and capabilities that make it indispensable for organizations.
Data Consistency and Integrity:
MDG enforces data standards, policies, and rules to maintain consistent and accurate master data across systems, departments, and business processes.
Data Quality Management:
MDG enables organizations to define data quality metrics, and perform data cleansing, deduplication, and validation to improve data accuracy and completeness.
Regulatory Compliance:
MDG helps organizations comply with regulatory requirements such as GDPR, HIPAA, and industry-specific regulations by establishing data governance policies, consent management, and data protection measures.
Data Stewardship:
MDG assigns data stewards responsible for data ownership, policy enforcement, and resolving data-related issues, ensuring accountability and better data management.
Improved Decision-Making:
With accurate and reliable master data, organizations can make informed decisions, enhance operational efficiency, and gain a competitive edge in the market.
Master Data Governance Best Practices & Tools
To successfully implement MDG, organizations should follow these best practices in mdm data governance:
Establish a Governance Framework
Master data governance framework defines clear roles, responsibilities, and processes for data governance, including data stewardship, data ownership, and data lifecycle management.
Data Standardization and Harmonization
Develop data standards, naming conventions, and data models to ensure consistency and compatibility across systems.
Data Quality Management
Implement data quality processes, including data profiling, cleansing, and monitoring, to continuously improve data accuracy and reliability.
Change Management
Develop a change management strategy to facilitate organizational buy-in, user adoption, and ongoing improvement of MDG practices.
Leverage Technology Solutions
Deploy MDG software tools and platforms to automate data governance processes, streamline workflows, and enable better collaboration among stakeholders.
Master Data Governance (MDG) is a critical discipline that enables organizations to manage their master data effectively, ensuring consistency, accuracy, and reliability. By implementing a robust master data governance framework, organizations can drive data-driven decision-making, enhance operational efficiency, and comply with regulatory requirements.
In today’s data-driven business environment, organizations cannot afford to overlook the importance of Master Data Governance. It plays a crucial role in ensuring data quality, consistency, and integrity, which are fundamental for successful operations, informed decision-making, and improved customer experiences. By implementing robust Master Data Governance practices, organizations can harness the full potential of their data assets and gain a competitive edge in the dynamic marketplace of the digital age.

Microservices and Master Data Management (MDM)
Table Of Contents
usinesses today are turning to microservices and master data management (MDM) to keep up with the fast-paced and ever-changing digital landscape. Data Management Microservices provide unmatched flexibility to businesses by breaking down monolithic applications into small, autonomous services that work together to form a composable enterprise. However, this also presents challenges in data management. That’s where MDM comes in, ensuring that the data stored in data management microservices remains consistent and relevant by cleansing and discarding redundant and obsolete data. By incorporating data management microservices and master data management into their digital transformation strategies, businesses can streamline their processes and stay ahead of the competition.
What are Microservices
Microservices are a type of autonomous, small services that can be linked together to form a more streamlined business process. They function as individual packaged business capabilities, or they can work together to create a more complex process. Although they communicate with each other, they don’t share execution contexts. Microservices serve as the building blocks for larger application suites and are simpler to develop and deploy compared to monolithic applications or service-oriented architectures. They use simple HTTP protocols with XML or JSON and are API driven. This makes them more flexible in their scalability and composability. However, the potential downside is that a microservice ecosystem can become too complex too quickly. To mitigate this risk, it’s important to link them together using API, which can create packaged business capabilities.
What is a Microservice example?
Amazon’s evolution from a monolithic architecture to a microservices architecture serves as a prime example of the benefits of the latter. In the past, Amazon’s services were tightly coupled together, similar to many startup architectures. However, today, Amazon has adopted a more microservice-oriented approach, where most of its services operate independently of each other. This shift has resulted in increased flexibility, scalability, and streamlined business processes. Other companies are also utilizing microservices to achieve similar advantages.
What is Master Data Management?
Maintaining accurate and relevant data is crucial for any business. It is here that Master Data Management (MDM) comes into play. MDM is the process of ensuring data quality by eliminating redundant and obsolete data. By implementing MDM strategies, businesses can keep their data architecture consistent and up-to-date. This helps maintain a single source of truth, ensuring that decisions are based on reliable and accurate information.
Microservices vs MDM OR Microservices with MDM
Microservices and Master Data Management (MDM) Architecture are two concepts that have been gaining a lot of attention in recent years. Combining the two concepts can lead to a more efficient and scalable MDM Microservices Architecture.
Benefit 1
One of the key benefits of using a MDM microservices architecture is that it enables greater flexibility and agility. By breaking down MDM into smaller, independent services, businesses can more easily adapt to changes in their data environment. For example, if a new data source is introduced, it can be easily integrated into the MDM architecture without disrupting the entire system.
Benefit 2​
Another benefit of using MDM microservices architecture is that it enables more efficient data governance. By separating the various data entities and processes into smaller, more manageable services, businesses can more easily monitor and control their data. This is especially important when dealing with sensitive data, such as personally identifiable information (PII) or financial data.
Benefit 3​
Using a MDM microservices architecture can also lead to better scalability and performance. Because each service is independent, businesses can more easily scale individual services up or down as needed. This can help to improve performance and reduce latency, which is especially important when dealing with large amounts of data
Challenge
Despite the benefits, there are also some potential challenges associated with using master data management in a microservices architecture. One of the main challenges is the increased complexity of the overall system. With many small, independent services, it can be difficult to keep track of how the various services interact with one another. This can lead to increased overhead in terms of monitoring, testing, and debugging.
Conclusion
Overall, however, the benefits of using master data management in microservices far outweigh the potential challenges. By breaking down MDM into smaller, more manageable services, businesses can achieve greater flexibility, agility, and scalability in their data management processes. As such, it is no surprise that many businesses are increasingly adopting this approach of Master Data Management in Microservices to improve their data management capabilities.

Unveiling the Distinctions: Reference Data Management vs Master Data Management
Table Of Contents
When it comes to data management, it’s important to know the differences between Reference and Master Data Management. Many people use the terms interchangeably, but they are actually two separate things. Understanding the differences between the two is crucial to making the right decisions when it comes to your data management strategy. In this blog post, we’ll be examining Reference Data Management vs. Master Data Management to help you determine which is the right approach for your business needs.
What is Reference Data Management?
Reference Data Management involves the management of data elements that provide context or categorization to other data. It represents the static values used for classification, validation, and control purposes. Examples of reference data include
country codes, currency codes, product categories, industry codes
, etc. RDM focuses on maintaining the accuracy, consistency, and integrity of reference data throughout an organization. The goal of reference data management is to ensure consistency, accuracy, and reliability of reference data across the organization. By establishing a centralized repository for reference data and implementing proper
governance
processes, RDM enables data analysts, data scientists, and other stakeholders to access and utilize high-quality reference data for their analysis and decision-making.
What is Master Data Management?
Master Data Management
focuses on managing critical business entities, such as
customers, products, employees, and suppliers,
to ensure consistency and accuracy across various systems and applications. MDM aims to create a single, trusted source of master data, eliminating redundancies and inconsistencies that may arise from data silos. It establishes a unified view of master data, enabling better decision-making and improved operational efficiency. The primary objective of MDM is to ensure that master data is accurate, reliable, and consistent across various systems and applications within an organization. By establishing a central repository for master data, MDM enables different departments and systems to access and use the same set of trusted and up-to-date information. MDM also involves establishing data governance policies, roles, and responsibilities to ensure the ongoing management maintenance and quality control of the master data.
Key Differences Between RDM vs MDM:
Scope and Focus
RDM primarily focuses on managing specific reference data sets that enhance the context and validity of other data elements. On the other hand, MDM aims to govern and unify all reference master data within an enterprise, including customer data, product information, and more.
Data Management Objectives:
RDM focuses on maintaining the quality, accuracy, and consistency of reference data, ensuring its relevance and usability. MDM, while also addressing these objectives, aims to create a centralized, authoritative source for master data, allowing organizations to eliminate data silos and improve data governance.
Integration and Governance:
RDM often operates within the context of MDM, serving as a critical component. MDM provides the overarching framework for data governance, enabling the integration and management of multiple data domains.
Data Hierarchy:
RDM exists as a subset of MDM, focusing on reference data elements, while MDM encompasses both master reference data, providing a holistic approach to data management.
Importance of Reference Data Management:
Reference data provides the contextual information needed to interpret and categorize operational data within an organization. It includes codes, classifications, standards, and other non-transactional data elements. Effective RDM ensures that reference data is accurately defined, consistently used, and accessible across various systems and applications. The importance of RDM lies in:
Ensuring Data Consistency:
By centralizing and standardizing reference data, RDM promotes consistency in data interpretation and usage, reducing the risk of data inconsistencies and errors.
Supporting Data Integration:
RDM facilitates the integration of reference data from different sources, enabling systems and applications to work cohesively by using a shared set of reference data.
Improving Decision-Making:
Reliable and well-managed reference data helps organizations make informed decisions based on accurate and consistent information.
Importance of Master Data Management:
Master data refers to critical data entities that are essential for an organization’s operations, such as customers, products, and employees. MDM aims to establish a single, authoritative source of master data to ensure its accuracy, integrity, and consistency. The importance of MDM includes:
Enhancing Data Quality:
MDM processes improve data quality by
removing duplicates
, resolving inconsistencies, and validating data against predefined rules, ensuring accurate and reliable master data.
Supporting Business Processes:
Well-managed master data enables smooth business operations, enhances customer experiences, and supports various processes such as sales, marketing, and supply chain management.
Enabling Data Governance:
MDM establishes data governance frameworks, policies, and stewardship roles to ensure ongoing data management, quality control, and compliance with regulations.
Facilitating Integration and Interoperability:
MDM enables the integration of master data across systems, applications, and departments, supporting data sharing and interoperability.
In conclusion,
the differences between rdm vs mdm and their importance in data governance cannot be overstated. It is essential to have a robust Reference and Master Data Management strategy in place, as they play a crucial role in ensuring data consistency, improving decision-making, supporting regulatory
compliance
and risk mitigation efforts, and enhancing operational efficiency.

What is data localization and data privacy?

Introducing Posidex’s Zero Knowledge Proof (ZKP) Data Vault
This circles us back to the new approach: the Zero Knowledge Proof (ZKP) Data Vault.
ZKP concept comes from Blockchain.
It is an increasingly common way of achieving privacy in public blockchain networks.
It’s a method where one party cryptographically proves to another that they possess knowledge about a piece of information without revealing the actual underlying information.
Requestor ( who is making the request) gets the insights & can perform analytics, without having access to the plain text data with a Yes or No answer or a value.

Watchlist Screening: A Crucial Component in AML Compliance
Table Of Contents
Global financial crime continues to escalate.
India alone has suffered online financial losses amounting to approximately ₹8,500 crore. Alarmingly, more than half of these losses are tied to cybercrime. This surge in financial crimes has increased the compliance burden for financial institutions (FIs). What FIs need is a robust security checkpoint. A frontier that keeps them compliant and
maintains integrity, trust, and reputation
.  This is where a global watchlist screening solution emerges as a vital component.
In India, the total volume of penalties levied by RBI was
INR 54.78 crore
in FY 25 for non-compliance.
In July 2025, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) imposed more than
S$28 million
on nine financial institutions (FIs) for breaches of its AML/CFT requirements.
In the European Union, fines for anti-money laundry (AML) breaches vary by country but can reach €5 million or up to 10% of annual turnover.
In UAE, Corporate fines can reach
AED 50 million
for money laundering offenses, and penalties for general AML breaches range from AED 10,000 to AED 1,000,000
What is watchlist screening
AML compliance regulations mandate that financial institutions have to rigorously check new and existing customers to stop money laundering.
Watchlist screening
functions as the primary line of defense, ensuring that businesses do not inadvertently onboard customers or entities that may pose harm.
By cross-referencing data
during onboarding or on an ad hoc basis
, it screens customers and identifies risky individuals to successfully meet legal regulations. This meticulous vetting process covers diverse watchlists, including AML, politically exposed persons (PEPs), sanctioned individuals, and entities associated with criminal activities.
The cost of non-AML compliance
For FIs, watchlist screening is a regulatory obligation.  If you fail to do so, you not only become instrumental in money laundering but also
damage your reputation
and public image. Not being AML-compliant comes with
hefty compliance fines
too.
‍
The cost of overall financial crime compliance is nearly
$61 billion
in the US and Canada, while in the APAC region, it’s $45 billion.With the impending Anti-Money-Laundering Authority (
AMLA)
, the cost of compliance in the EU can reach as high
as £1 million
.
Fuzzy-Logic Name Matching During Screening
Traditional, manual screening systems often fail due to:
Human errors and high risk of false positives
Minor spelling or transliteration differences
Typos, aliases, or phonetic variations
Relying solely on syntax or sound—but not both
Our automated screening tool takes a more nuanced approach to screening by using fuzzy logic. Moreover, it also searches for
phonetic similarities,
the results are even more precise. This guarantees that you don’t accidentally vet out a customer just because their name is similar to that of a sanctioned person or criminal.
1. Syntax and phonetic matching
Powered by a robust algorithm and a powerful, multidimensional watchlist database, it offers:
Comprehensive Name Matching
Uses fuzzy logic to account for alternate spellings (e.g., “Muhammad” vs “Mohammed”), aliases, transliteration (Arabic–English, Tamil to English, or any other), and typos.
Dual Matching Techniques
Unlike many systems that use either syntax-based or phonetic matching, ours applies both simultaneously—minimizing false positives and false negatives.
High Precision, Minimal Noise
Thanks to advanced AI/ML tuning and our deep watchlist database (2,100+ global/regional sources), we deliver market-leading accuracy with very low false-positive rates.
2. Real-time & ongoing screening
Accurately, identifying high-risk entities is one side of the AML compliance coin. The other is speed.  Financial institutions need to be proactive, not reactive. For that, you want real-time and
ongoing monitoring
of customers. An
always-on
watchlist screening solution regularly updates watchlists so you have the latest information at your disposal to mitigate
emerging
risks swiftly
and
be alerted to any
change in the risk status
of existing customers. Our watchlist solution rescans customers automatically, sending alerts only when an actual risk emerges—maintaining both compliance and customer experience.
‍
Your watchlist screening solution shouldn’t raise a red flag just for the sake of it. A good screening solution would only file a SAR when it contains adequate information to warrant the filing of the notice.
Our advanced technology
enables thorough customer due diligence and enhanced due diligence without causing unnecessary delays. Customizable risk thresholds and setting screening parameters based on risk appetite avoid the creation of excessive suspicious activity reports (SARs).
3. Internal & third-party screening layers
Beyond global watchlists, your risk framework becomes far more resilient when you also:
Check against your organization’s own data
, screening existing CRM or rejected-customer lists for internal fraud signals.
Cross-verify with third-party data sources
, such as peer bank watchlists or consortium data, for broader visibility into emerging risks.
Our screening tool supports both these layers, driving deeper insights while keeping compliance airtight.
The Takeaway
In an age of heightened regulatory oversight and cross-border risk, investing in an
AI-powered watchlist screening solution
i
sn't just smart. It’s essential.
Posidex’s global watchlist name screening solution uses best-in-class technology relied on by Tier 1 corporations for screening against 2100+ lists. It seamlessly integrates with your existing systems, enabling real-time screening and instant response without disrupting daily operations or compromising efficiency.
Safeguard your institution, screen smarter, not just harder.

The Challenge
: Fragmented identities across businesses
For large retail chains with multiple lines of business (LoBs), like our client, a single customer often exists in multiple systems: jewelry, watches, eyewear, or wearables. Each maintains their own data. The result is data chaos:
Multiple customer IDs for the same person
Ineffective loyalty programs
Poor cross-selling opportunities
Fragmented customer experience
Without a unique customer ID for each customer across business lines, the organization couldn’t track total customer value, recognize repeat buyers, or personalize marketing effectively.
In a competitive retail landscape, the brand knew the next leap in customer experience required a common customer identity system that could unify data from across its verticals in real time.
Where CDPs fall short and why MDM is the missing layer
Like most global retailers, the client had already invested in a CDP (Customer Data Platform) to centralize and activate customer data for marketing. But CDPs depend entirely on the quality of data that flows into them. When upstream data is fragmented, duplicated, or inconsistent, CDPs struggle to build accurate customer profiles.
Many enterprises initially treat MDM as a backend function. But when matched with a CDP, MDM becomes a strategic asset.
It reduces data chaos at the source
It strengthens campaign ROI
It helps teams trust their data
It accelerates digital transformation across the organization
A CDP enhanced with Master Data Management (MDM)  becomes dramatically more intelligent and reliable.

that CDPs lack. By unifying and cleansing customer identities first, MDM turns the CDP from a data collector into a truly intelligent engine. You unlock:
Accurate, unified customer profiles.
Sharper audience segmentation.
Stronger personalization in every channel.
More efficient marketing spends.
Better attribution models and insights.
A richer, more dependable Customer 360

Implementing
world's largest deduplication
on a whopping 750 Million Customer Data
Now, let’s rewind and delve deeper into how Posidex implemented arguably the largest customer MDM solution globally that too, at an incredibly low TCO.
Posidex Customer MDM gave to the Indian insurance giant which is probably the world’s biggest in terms of policies, a staggering leap in operational velocity, allowing for daily policy synchronisations and real-time query capability.
The need was to do de-duplication of 750 million Customer policies and create unique customers and then link new policy data with master data on a daily basis, so that Customer data is clean, accurate, and up-to-date for better insights and customer serviceability.
Problem Statement
Solution
Results
A persisting Challenge
faced by Insurance companies globally
In the insurance industry, efficient cross-sell and quick claim processing aren't just nice to have. It's crucial for happy customers and a thriving business.
And you can't do that without updated, accurate information about each customer. But as the customer base increases, connecting all the data points to achieve unique customer identification for achieving business goals (happy customers and growth) gets complicated. Compounding this complexity are the shifting life stages of customers, with changing addresses & phone numbers due to relocations and sometimes even changes in surname modifications following marriage.
This is a universal problem faced by every BFSI organization across the world, including our client.
A
data maze
of epic proportions
With an impressive 750+ million customer policies under its belt, the insurance giant is probably the world’s biggest in terms of policies. Let’s put that number into better perspective: it’s 2.5 times the total life insurance policies in force in the USA, or more than the entire population of Europe.
However, customer data had duplicates, inaccuracies, and inconsistencies across various customer elements like names, birthdates, addresses, phone numbers, and the use of different identification documents. A customer master data management (MDM) solution from a global MNC was implemented sometime ago to create & update a unique Customer base. While some of the data issues were resolved, some major challenges persisted.
Some customers still ended up with duplicate Customer IDs because the solution could not handle all the variations in data elements.
The system was unable to handle large data volumes, so policy updates lagged. It synced new policies periodically, a far cry from the real-time updates the industry needs.
Innovation at scale:
the need
To overcome the above, Customer decided to migrate to a new customer MDM solution that could:
Process existing 750 million policies afresh to create a new, unique customer base through automated process without manual intervention.
Ensure the daily synchronization of new policies. To be done in 5 hours.
Real Time query capability on the entire Customer base.
Utilize an open-source database and X86-based commodity servers, so the costs are low while meeting performance requirements.
Global search by the Client for
best solution
A global tender was floated for a solution to meet the above requirements.After a rigorous evaluation process, the client shortlisted 3 solutions and from these selected Posidex. Solution development commenced in 2021, and by 2022, the platform was live. Posidex's solution met all the needs and performance expectations of the client.
Unleashing
Transformative Results
To tackle the complexity of managing such a large amount of customer data, a proven solution i.e. Posidex Prime MDM Platform, with a proprietary AI/ML model was used which cut through such large data like a hot knife through butter. Since the volume is unprecedented, the new feature of Horizontal Scalability was implemented
Better customer ID unification:
It processed data, creating a unique customer base of 480 million from 750 million policy data, which is about 10% better.
Daily policy updates:
Daily new policies between 100,000 to 250,000 are synced with base data which was earlier done periodically. The processing was now reduced to a mere 3 to 4 hours, ensuring employees had instant access to the latest customer information.
The solution was implemented using an open-source database and cost-effective commodity hardware for production, UAT, and DR. Thus the TCO was remarkably low given such a large volume of data and the demanding computational needs of the project.
Continued Excellence
: Posidex Leading The Way Forward
Compared to similar solutions from global multinational companies, our solution gave the insurance firm near real-time data and rapid response, to drive the business with the lowest TCO with a near huge improvement in speed.

A telecom giant detects subscribers with multiple connections with

Posidex helped India's second-largest telecommunications provider meet stringent regulatory compliance and avoid hefty fines. Handling as much as over 50 million data points in some key regions, our AI-driven match engine empowered the telecom to accurately and promptly detect if a subscriber held multiple connections right at the moment of providing a new connection.
This real-time subscriber verification and identification of bulk subscriber connections reported 200% more correct matches in record time.
Problem Statement
Solution
Results
The Challenge
: Compliance with stringent regulatory norms
For telecom operators, maintaining an accurate record of subscriber connections is a legal mandate. India's Telecom Regulatory Authority (TRAI) requires companies to report the exact number of connections per subscriber each month. Any discrepancies result in severe financial penalties.
For our client, one of the world’s top mobile service providers with over
289 million customers
, this compliance requirement was a massive operational challenge. Processing millions of subscribers records every month required immense computing resources, and manpower. Identifying bulk connections from the same subscriber was difficult due to data quality issues and slowed turnaround time.
The regulatory authority required timely and precise reporting, increasing pressure on manual verification teams. Subscriber verification in sensitive areas lacked efficiency due to inadequate real-time verification.
Failure to accurately verify and report a potential subscriber with over 9 connections (bulk connections) put the telecom provider at risk of incurring multi-million-dollar penalties.
The solution
: AI-powered subscriber identification
After a rigorous evaluation process, the telecom company selected Posidex’s
PrimeMatch
TM
and
SetMatch
TM
to transform its subscriber verification and compliance reporting.
When onboarding a new subscriber, the telecom matched their information with the total subscriber base within a circle, known as LTD (live-to-date), using SetMatch
TM
. It performed bulk deduplication in batches. Matching and putting the results in TRAI mandated clusters.
For subscribers added on that day, known as FTD (for the day), PrimeMatch
TM
did real-time matching using an exposed synchronous API. It integrated instant subscriber verification within the workflow.
The solution also addressed underlying data quality issues, ensuring 99.5 % accuracy in matching. It automated reporting format compliance with TERM regulations.

With Posidex’s technology, the telecom provider detected previously missed bulk connections with greater precision, identifying 200% more matches. Accurate and timely compliance reporting in the format required by the TERM eliminated the risk of fines. Processing vast data volumes efficiently, reducing infrastructure costs. Seamless real-time verification enabled instant KYC and regulatory compliance in sensitive areas.

and SetMatch

, the telecom provider didn’t just meet compliance requirements—they transformed how subscriber data was managed. The enhanced process efficiency improved regulatory adherence, and optimized infrastructure.

Frequently asked questions
What does Posidex do for the Banking & Financial Services Industry?
With over two decades of experience as a deep-tech enterprise, we provide future-ready, privacy-enhancing customer data solutions that meet GDPR, DPD & Data residency laws while empowering businesses with contextual and actionable customer insights in real-time.
How does Posidex deliver privacy-enhanced customer insights?
Our proprietary mathematical algorithm uses VEARE (Vectorized, Encoded, Anonymized, Randomized, and Encrypted) tokens. These tokens keep customer data secure and private at all stages of processing and sharing.
How do Banking & Financial Service organizations leverage real-time entity match?
Banking and financial services leverage the Posidex PrimeMDM suite for risk management, fraud reduction, regulatory compliance, comprehensive customer view, cost reduction and overall business growth.
Does Posidex customize the solution bundle for specific banking and financial service needs?
Yes, we offer customized AI/ML-supported solutions for data quality & management, regulatory compliance, network analysis, entity resolution, and risk management.
What are the configuration and training requirements for implementing Posidex solutions?
Our solutions have intuitive UI which is highly configurable with existing systems and requires minimal training.

Customer Linking & Identification Process
Effortlessly identify, link, and merge customer data at scale
Get a demo
Challenge
Clean and connected data to operate your organization at scale
Finding the same or similar customer records in mountains of customer data is easy when there is a common identifier between them, like a name, PAN, or SSN. Linking customer records, that too at scale, becomes a challenge when there is no consistent identifier.
You need to build complex rules with different weights and scores to determine matches. Based on the results, records are linked together and checked to see if they are indeed the same entity or not.
Product Overview
A Deduplication Marvel
CLIP (Customer Linking & Identification Process) is a bulk entity search and match product. What makes CLIP a marvel among other deduplication products is that it can establish linkages between customer records:
- from disparate data sources
-
even
when there is no overlapping identifier across data sources
- The quantity of duplicate records is large
It looks for similar demographics and other anonymous identifiers. All the while ensuring customer data privacy.
